claim: p130Cas contains two intrinsically disordered regions associated with LLPS.
source: Examination of the p130Cas amino acid sequence revealed two intrinsically disordered regions of the type often associated with LLPS (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on computational prediction of disorder probability shown in Figure 1A

claim: The substrate domain of p130Cas forms the largest unstructured region.
source: The substrate domain, which contains 15 tyrosines potentially phosphorylated by src family kinases, forms the largest unstructured region, while a segment of the C-terminal domain is also disordered.
evidence: Based on disorder prediction analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Transfected EGFP-p130Cas protein was expressed at approximately 4-5 times endogenous levels.
source: Western blotting cell lysates for p130Cas and correcting for transfection efficiency showed that the transfected protein was ~4–5 x endogenous (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Small spots of p130Cas emerge from focal adhesions and move into the cytoplasm.
source: Live imaging revealed that, in addition to its localization to focal adhesions, small spots of p130Cas emerged from focal adhesions and moved into the cytoplasm and sometimes back to focal adhesions (Videos 1–3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Videos 1-3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: p130Cas cytoplasmic spots are observed in CHO, HeLa, and HEK293T cells.
source: CHO, HeLa, and HEK293T cells showed similar behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F

claim: MCF7 cells show cytoplasmic p130Cas spots without overexpression.
source: Staining for endogenous p130Cas did not show obvious cytoplasmic droplets in untransfected MEFs, however, MCF7 cells, which have ~2–2.5 x higher endogenous p130Cas than NIH3T3, showed cytoplasmic spots without overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H

claim: p130Cas spots merge to form single circular droplets.
source: Spots were observed merging to form a single circular droplet (Figure 1C), a behavior typical of LLPS.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging showing droplet fusion in Figure 1C

claim: p130Cas droplet area increases over 24 hours after cell plating.
source: Droplet area increases over 24 hr after cell plating (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Quantification of droplet area at 6 hr and 24 hr shown in Figure 1D

claim: At 6 hours after plating, p130Cas droplets show rapid fluorescence recovery with t1/2 of 9.4±1.9 seconds and mobile fraction of approximately 72%.
source: At 6 hr after plating, photobleached EGFP-p130Cas droplets recovered rapidly (t1/2 = 9.4±1.9 s, mobile fraction ~72%; Figure 1E, G and H).
evidence: FRAP data shown in Figure 1E, G, and H

claim: At 24 hours after plating, p130Cas droplets show slower fluorescence recovery with t1/2 of 26.4±3.7 seconds and mobile fraction of approximately 26%.
source: FRAP at 24 after plating showed markedly slower recovery (t1/2 = 26.4±3.7 s, mobile fraction ~26%; Figure 1F–I).
evidence: FRAP data shown in Figure 1F–I

claim: Rapid molecular exchange at 6 hours and decreased exchange over time support p130Cas LLPS in cells.
source: Both the rapid molecular exchange at 6 hr and the decreased exchange over time support p130Cas LLPS in cells.
evidence: FRAP measurements showing time-dependent changes in recovery kinetics

claim: Hexanediol treatment disrupts p130Cas droplets.
source: We observed disruption of droplets after the addition of hexanediol (Figure 1J&K) and enhanced droplet assembly after the addition of ammonium acetate (Figure 1L and M; Jain and Vale, 2017), again, behaviors typical of phase separations.
evidence: Imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1J&K

claim: Ammonium acetate treatment enhances p130Cas droplet assembly.
source: We observed disruption of droplets after the addition of hexanediol (Figure 1J&K) and enhanced droplet assembly after the addition of ammonium acetate (Figure 1L and M; Jain and Vale, 2017), again, behaviors typical of phase separations.
evidence: Imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1L and M, with citation to Jain and Vale, 2017

claim: p130Cas forms cytoplasmic condensates outside focal adhesions.
source: We conclude that p130Cas forms cytoplasmic condensates outside focal adhesions.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including fusion behavior, FRAP dynamics, and response to polarity-altering reagents

claim: Paxillin co-localizes with p130Cas in cytoplasmic spots.
source: Imaging at a focal plane through the nucleus and above the basal surface revealed strong co-localization of these proteins with p130Cas in cytoplasmic spots (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: FAK co-localizes with p130Cas in cytoplasmic spots.
source: Imaging at a focal plane through the nucleus and above the basal surface revealed strong co-localization of these proteins with p130Cas in cytoplasmic spots (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: Paxillin co-emerges from focal adhesions along with p130Cas.
source: Paxillin (Figure 2E, Video 4) and FAK (Figure 2F, Video 5) co-emerged from focal adhesions along with p130Cas, indicating correlated dynamics.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2E and Video 4

claim: FAK co-emerges from focal adhesions along with p130Cas.
source: Paxillin (Figure 2E, Video 4) and FAK (Figure 2F, Video 5) co-emerged from focal adhesions along with p130Cas, indicating correlated dynamics.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2F and Video 5

claim: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets form normally in paxillin-null MEFs.
source: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets formed normally in both of these cell lines (Figure 2G and H), indicating that neither was required for p130Cas phase separation.
evidence: Imaging of EGFP-p130Cas in paxillin-null cells shown in Figure 2G

claim: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets form normally in FAK-null MEFs.
source: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets formed normally in both of these cell lines (Figure 2G and H), indicating that neither was required for p130Cas phase separation.
evidence: Imaging of EGFP-p130Cas in FAK-null cells shown in Figure 2H

claim: Paxillin is not required for p130Cas phase separation.
source: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets formed normally in both of these cell lines (Figure 2G and H), indicating that neither was required for p130Cas phase separation.
evidence: Droplet formation in paxillin-null cells shown in Figure 2G

claim: FAK is not required for p130Cas phase separation.
source: Cytoplasmic p130Cas droplets formed normally in both of these cell lines (Figure 2G and H), indicating that neither was required for p130Cas phase separation.
evidence: Droplet formation in FAK-null cells shown in Figure 2H

claim: Cytoplasmic droplets are not evident when tagged paxillin is expressed in p130Cas-null MEFs.
source: By contrast, when tagged paxillin or FAK were expressed in p130Cas-null MEFs, cytoplasmic droplets were not evident (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Imaging of tagRFP-paxillin in p130Cas-null cells shown in Figure 2I

claim: Cytoplasmic droplets are not evident when tagged FAK is expressed in p130Cas-null MEFs.
source: By contrast, when tagged paxillin or FAK were expressed in p130Cas-null MEFs, cytoplasmic droplets were not evident (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Imaging of mcherry-FAK in p130Cas-null cells shown in Figure 2J

claim: p130Cas is the main driver of phase separation outside focal adhesions.
source: These data argue that p130Cas is the main driver of phase separation outside focal adhesions.
evidence: Droplet formation requires p130Cas but not paxillin or FAK, as shown in Figure 2G-J

claim: p130Cas within droplets is phosphorylated on substrate domain tyrosines.
source: Cells expressing EGFP-p130Cas stained for pY-Cas using a specific antibody (Yaginuma et al., 2020) revealed strong staining of condensates as well as focal adhesions (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2K–M with citation to Yaginuma et al., 2020

claim: The ratio of phosphorylated p130Cas to total p130Cas is drastically higher in focal adhesions compared to droplets.
source: We noticed, however, that pY-Cas staining relative to total p130Cas intensity was drastically higher in focal adhesions compared to droplets (Figure 2N).
evidence: Quantification of pY-Cas/total p130Cas ratio shown in Figure 2N

claim: p130Cas is much less phosphorylated in droplets than in focal adhesions.
source: This result suggests that p130Cas is much less phosphorylated in droplets than in focal adhesions.
evidence: Ratio analysis shown in Figure 2N

claim: Mutation of substrate domain tyrosines to phenylalanine modestly decreases droplet formation.
source: Mutation of substrate domain tyrosines modestly decreased, deletion of the substrate domain strongly decreased, and deletion of the C-terminal disordered sequence had no effect on droplet formation (Figure 2P and Q).
evidence: Quantification of droplet-positive cells for Y15F mutant shown in Figure 2P and Q

claim: Deletion of the substrate domain strongly decreases droplet formation.
source: Mutation of substrate domain tyrosines modestly decreased, deletion of the substrate domain strongly decreased, and deletion of the C-terminal disordered sequence had no effect on droplet formation (Figure 2P and Q).
evidence: Quantification of droplet-positive cells for ΔSD mutant shown in Figure 2P and Q

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal disordered sequence has no effect on droplet formation.
source: Mutation of substrate domain tyrosines modestly decreased, deletion of the substrate domain strongly decreased, and deletion of the C-terminal disordered sequence had no effect on droplet formation (Figure 2P and Q).
evidence: Quantification of droplet-positive cells for C-term deletion mutant shown in Figure 2P and Q

claim: The substrate domain is the main driver of p130Cas phase separation.
source: Thus, while the substrate domain is the main driver of phase separation, its tyrosine phosphorylation contributes to this effect to a lesser extent.
evidence: Deletion of substrate domain strongly reduces droplets while Y to F mutation has modest effect, as shown in Figure 2P and Q

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of the substrate domain contributes to phase separation to a lesser extent than the domain itself.
source: Thus, while the substrate domain is the main driver of phase separation, its tyrosine phosphorylation contributes to this effect to a lesser extent.
evidence: Y15F mutation modestly decreases droplet formation compared to strong decrease with substrate domain deletion, as shown in Figure 2P and Q

claim: The Y to F mutant substrate domain shows no change in intrinsic disorder.
source: The Y to F mutant substrate domain showed no change in intrinsic disorder (Figure 2R), consistent with roles for both phosphorylation-dependent and -independent interactions.
evidence: Disorder probability plot for WT and Y15F mutant shown in Figure 2R

claim: Ammonium acetate treatment increases RFP-paxillin signal around EGFP-p130Cas beads.
source: We observed a low but detectable RFP-paxillin signal around EGFP-p130Cas beads under control conditions, a large increase after the addition of ammonium acetate and a decrease after the addition of hexanediol (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Imaging of beads shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Hexanediol treatment decreases RFP-paxillin signal around EGFP-p130Cas beads.
source: We observed a low but detectable RFP-paxillin signal around EGFP-p130Cas beads under control conditions, a large increase after the addition of ammonium acetate and a decrease after the addition of hexanediol (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Imaging of beads shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: No paxillin fluorescence is observed around EGFP-only beads under any treatment conditions.
source: No paxillin fluorescence was observed around EGFP-only beads under any of these conditions.
evidence: Imaging of EGFP-only control beads shown in Figure 3B

claim: The bead-based assay allows specific assembly of condensed phases on bead-bound p130Cas.
source: These results suggest a specific assembly of condensed phases on the bead-bound p130Cas.
evidence: Differential paxillin recruitment to p130Cas vs EGFP beads shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Out of 78 proteins reported to interact directly with p130Cas, 30 were enriched in the condensates.
source: Out of the 78 proteins reported to interact directly with p130Cas (Evans et al., 2017), 30 were enriched in the condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Venn diagram shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with citation to Evans et al., 2017

claim: The most prominent Gene Ontology terms for proteins isolated on EGFP-p130Cas beads are protein synthesis, RNA splicing, and RNA processing.
source: For the proteins specifically isolated on EGFP-p130Cas beads, the most prominent Gene Ontology (GO) terms for biological processes identified protein synthesis, RNA splicing, and RNA processing (Figure 3E).
evidence: Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: p130Cas shows little correlation with the stress granule marker G3BP2 without arsenite treatment.
source: p130Cas showed little correlation with the stress granule marker G3BP2, either without or with arsenite treatment to induce their assembly (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A–D

claim: p130Cas shows little correlation with the stress granule marker G3BP2 with arsenite treatment.
source: p130Cas showed little correlation with the stress granule marker G3BP2, either without or with arsenite treatment to induce their assembly (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A–D

claim: Of six major stress granule constituents, only PABPC1 was detected in p130Cas condensates.
source: We also saw that of the six major stress granule constituents CAPRIN1, PRRC2C, USP10, UBAP2L, and CSDE1 (Yang et al., 2020) and PABPC1 (Kedersha et al., 2000) only PABPC1 was detected in p130Cas condensates (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1 with citations to Yang et al., 2020 and Kedersha et al., 2000

claim: PABP does not colocalize with p130Cas droplets immediately after induction of stress granules.
source: Poly(A)-binding protein (PABP), which can be present in stress granules, did not colocalize with p130Cas droplets immediately after induction of stress granules (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: Argonaute 2 (Ago2) partially overlaps with p130Cas-positive LLPS after arsenite treatment.
source: However, argonaute 2 (Ago2), which is critical for miRNA-dependent mRNA regulation (Ender and Meister, 2010) and is a constituent of stress granules (and p-bodies), partially overlapped with p130Cas-positive LLPS after arsenite treatment (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4G and H with citation to Ender and Meister, 2010

claim: Dcp1A shows no overlap with p130Cas droplets.
source: Dcp1A, a critical component of p-bodies, showed no overlap with p130Cas droplets (Figure 4I–L & Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4I–L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: p130Cas condensates share some constituents but are distinct from both stress granules and p-bodies.
source: We conclude that p130Cas condensates share some constituents but are distinct from both stress granules and p-bodies.
evidence: Limited colocalization with stress granule and p-body markers shown in Figure 4

claim: Ago2 is concentrated in the center of p130Cas droplets.
source: Ago2 is concentrated in the center of the droplets (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging and line profile shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: GW182 is present in the outer rim of p130Cas structures.
source: GW182, which, like Ago2, is a component of the RISC complex that mediates miRNA-directed mRNA cleavage (Ding and Han, 2007), was present in the outer rim of p130Cas structures (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging and line profile shown in Figure 5C and D with citation to Ding and Han, 2007

claim: Messenger RNAs yield strong positive signals within a subset of p130Cas droplets in cells.
source: Messenger RNAs, which were localized by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using poly-T probes, yielded strong positive signals within a subset of p130Cas droplets in cells (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: RNA FISH imaging shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: Cycloheximide treatment decreases p130Cas LLPS.
source: CHX decreased p130Cas LLPS (Figure 5G&H).
evidence: Imaging and quantification of droplets after CHX treatment shown in Figure 5G&H

claim: p130Cas condensates may regulate translation or other aspects of mRNA metabolism.
source: Together, these results in Figure 5 suggest that p130Cas condensates may regulate translation or other aspects of mRNA metabolism.
evidence: Presence of RNA binding proteins, mRNAs, and response to CHX shown in Figure 5

claim: 297 mRNAs were enriched in p130Cas condensates by more than twofold with p-values less than 0.05.
source: RNAs that were enriched by > twofold with p-values <0.05 were considered positives (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2

claim: The most prominent Gene Ontology categories for genes enriched in p130Cas droplets are related to cell cycle progression, survival, and cell-cell communication.
source: The most prominent Gene Ontology categories for differentially isolated genes identified functions related to cell cycle progression, survival, and cell-cell communication (Figure 6B).
evidence: Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Out of 297 mRNAs present in p130Cas droplets, 46 were differentially regulated after overexpression of EGFP-p130Cas.
source: Out of 297 mRNAs present in p130Cas droplets, 46 were differentially regulated after overexpression of EGFP-p130Cas.
evidence: RNAseq comparison shown in Figure 6C and Supplementary file 3

claim: The probability of randomly choosing the 46 overlapping mRNAs is approximately less than 5%.
source: The probability of choosing these mRNAs at random is ~<5% (described in Methods), indicating a significant correlation between droplet-associated and differentially regulated mRNAs.
evidence: Statistical analysis described in Methods section

claim: There is a significant correlation between droplet-associated and differentially regulated mRNAs.
source: The probability of choosing these mRNAs at random is ~<5% (described in Methods), indicating a significant correlation between droplet-associated and differentially regulated mRNAs.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing <5% probability of random overlap

claim: Cell adhesion and inflammatory gene expression are the most strongly affected pathways by p130Cas overexpression.
source: Cell adhesion and inflammatory gene expression were the most strongly affected pathways (Figure 6D).
evidence: Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: MCF7 cells show more cytoplasmic droplets on higher fibronectin concentrations.
source: Again, focusing on a plane above the basal surface, we observed more cytoplasmic droplets on higher FN, as well as the expected increase in focal adhesions (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: Imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7A–C

claim: Translation decreases as a function of fibronectin coating density in MCF7 cells.
source: Staining cells for puromycin and quantifying integrated signal per cell showed that translation decreased as a function of FN coating density (Figure 7D and E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) cycloheximide treatment as a negative control for puromycin labeling.
evidence: Puromycin incorporation assay shown in Figure 7D and E

claim: Knockdown of p130Cas completely abrogates inhibition of translation on high fibronectin in MCF7 cells.
source: Knockdown of p130Cas completely abrogated inhibition of translation on high FN, indeed, after p130Cas knockdown, high FN modestly increased translation.
evidence: Puromycin assay after p130Cas knockdown shown in Figure 7F–H

claim: After p130Cas knockdown, high fibronectin modestly increases translation in MCF7 cells.
source: Knockdown of p130Cas completely abrogated inhibition of translation on high FN, indeed, after p130Cas knockdown, high FN modestly increased translation.
evidence: Puromycin assay after p130Cas knockdown shown in Figure 7F–H

claim: In HUVECs, translation decreases on high fibronectin.
source: In these cells, translation also decreased on high FN, which was again converted to an increase after p130Cas depletion.
evidence: Puromycin assay in HUVECs shown in Figure 7I-K

claim: In HUVECs, p130Cas depletion converts the decrease in translation on high fibronectin to an increase.
source: In these cells, translation also decreased on high FN, which was again converted to an increase after p130Cas depletion.
evidence: Puromycin assay after p130Cas knockdown in HUVECs shown in Figure 7I-K

claim: NIH3T3 cells show increased translation on high fibronectin with no effect of p130Cas knockdown.
source: By contrast, NIH3T3 cells that have lower levels of p130Cas (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G) showed increased translation on high FN, with no effect of p130Cas knockdown.
evidence: Puromycin assay in NIH3T3 cells shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G

claim: MCF10A cells show little change in puromycin labeling on low versus high fibronectin.
source: The differentiated breast epithelial line MCF10A, where p130Cas expression is low, also showed little change in puromycin labeling on low vs high FN (Figure 7L and M).
evidence: Puromycin assay in MCF10A cells shown in Figure 7L and M

claim: High p130Cas expression is required for a reduction in protein synthesis on high fibronectin.
source: Together, these results show that high p130Cas expression is required for a reduction in protein synthesis on high FN, an effect that correlates with droplet formation.
evidence: Comparison of cell lines with different p130Cas expression levels shown in Figure 7

claim: The reduction in protein synthesis on high fibronectin correlates with p130Cas droplet formation.
source: Together, these results show that high p130Cas expression is required for a reduction in protein synthesis on high FN, an effect that correlates with droplet formation.
evidence: Correlation between droplet formation and translation inhibition shown in Figure 7

claim: Blue light induces the formation of Cry2-p130Cas droplets that co-localize with paxillin.
source: In MCF7 cells expressing cry2-tagRFP-p130Cas, blue light-induced the formation of droplets that co-localized with paxillin and FAK, similar to native droplets (Figure 8A and B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Imaging of light-induced droplets shown in Figure 8A and B

claim: Blue light induces the formation of Cry2-p130Cas droplets that co-localize with FAK.
source: In MCF7 cells expressing cry2-tagRFP-p130Cas, blue light-induced the formation of droplets that co-localized with paxillin and FAK, similar to native droplets (Figure 8A and B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Imaging of light-induced droplets shown in Figure 8A and B

claim: MCF7 cells expressing Cry2-tagRFP-p130Cas kept in the dark behave similarly to control cells, with translation decreasing on high fibronectin.
source: MCF7 cells expressing this construct (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D) and kept in the dark behaved similarly to control cells, with translation decreasing on high FN (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Puromycin assay in dark conditions shown in Figure 8C and D

claim: Irradiation with 488 nm laser light for 0.5 seconds induces rapid Cry2-p130Cas droplet formation.
source: Irradiation with 488 nm laser light for 0.5 s induced rapid droplet formation, which in the absence of light then disassembled (t½ = ~9 min) (Figure 8E and F and Video 6).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after laser pulse shown in Figure 8E and F and Video 6

claim: Cry2-p130Cas droplets disassemble with a half-life of approximately 9 minutes in the absence of light.
source: Irradiation with 488 nm laser light for 0.5 s induced rapid droplet formation, which in the absence of light then disassembled (t½ = ~9 min) (Figure 8E and F and Video 6).
evidence: Quantification of droplet disassembly kinetics shown in Figure 8F

claim: Illumination of Cry2-p130Cas cells causes approximately 35% decrease in protein synthesis.
source: Puromycin labeling revealed ~35% dip in protein synthesis after illumination which in the dark gradually returned to initial levels (Figure 8I).
evidence: Puromycin assay after light induction shown in Figure 8I

claim: Protein synthesis gradually returns to initial levels after illumination is stopped.
source: Puromycin labeling revealed ~35% dip in protein synthesis after illumination which in the dark gradually returned to initial levels (Figure 8I).
evidence: Time course of puromycin labeling recovery shown in Figure 8I

claim: Prolonged intermittent illumination induces Cry2-p130Cas droplets and suppresses puromycin labeling for the duration of treatment.
source: Under this protocol, droplets were induced and puromycin labeling suppressed for the duration of the treatment (Figure 8J–L).
evidence: Imaging and puromycin assay during prolonged illumination shown in Figure 8J–L

claim: p130Cas droplet formation inhibits translation.
source: These experiments provide direct evidence that p130Cas droplet formation inhibits translation.
evidence: Light-induced droplet formation correlates with decreased translation shown in Figure 8

claim: LLPS has emerged as a major organizing principle in cells.
source: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as a major organizing principle in cells.
evidence: General statement about the field supported by subsequent citations

claim: Multiple components of integrin-mediated focal adhesions, including p130Cas, can form LLPS.
source: Recent work showed that multiple components of integrin-mediated focal adhesions, including p130Cas can form LLPS, which govern adhesion dynamics and related cell behaviors.
evidence: Reference to recent work in the field

claim: Focal adhesion-derived LLPS govern adhesion dynamics and related cell behaviors.
source: Recent work showed that multiple components of integrin-mediated focal adhesions, including p130Cas can form LLPS, which govern adhesion dynamics and related cell behaviors.
evidence: Reference to recent work in the field

claim: Plating cells on very high concentrations of fibronectin induces large focal adhesions.
source: Plating cells on very high concentrations of fibronectin to induce large focal adhesions inhibited message translation which required p130Cas and correlated with droplet formation.
evidence: Experimental design described in the abstract

claim: Plating cells on very high concentrations of fibronectin inhibits message translation.
source: Plating cells on very high concentrations of fibronectin to induce large focal adhesions inhibited message translation which required p130Cas and correlated with droplet formation.
evidence: Experimental results described in the abstract and shown in Figure 7

claim: Inhibition of message translation on high fibronectin requires p130Cas.
source: Plating cells on very high concentrations of fibronectin to induce large focal adhesions inhibited message translation which required p130Cas and correlated with droplet formation.
evidence: Knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7

claim: Photo-induction of p130Cas condensates using the Cry2 system reduces translation.
source: Photo-induction of p130Cas condensates using the Cry2 system also reduced translation.
evidence: Optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8

claim: High adhesion limits message translation via induction of p130Cas-dependent cytoplasmic LLPS.
source: These results identify a novel regulatory mechanism in which high adhesion limits message translation via induction of p130Cas-dependent cytoplasmic LLPS.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from Figures 7 and 8

claim: This mechanism may contribute to the quiescent state of very strongly adhesive myofibroblasts and senescent cells.
source: This mechanism may contribute to the quiescent state of very strongly adhesive myofibroblasts and senescent cells.
evidence: Speculation based on the findings and known biology of these cell types

claim: Under conditions of high adhesion and contractility, integrins drive the assembly of large focal adhesions that anchor contractile actomyosin stress fibers.
source: Under conditions of high adhesion and contractility, integrins drive the the assembly of large focal adhesions that anchor contractile actomyosin stress fibers, whereas, under conditions of lower adhesion or extracellular matrix stiffness, cells form smaller more dynamic adhesions.
evidence: Established knowledge about focal adhesion biology

claim: Under conditions of lower adhesion or extracellular matrix stiffness, cells form smaller more dynamic adhesions.
source: Under conditions of high adhesion and contractility, integrins drive the the assembly of large focal adhesions that anchor contractile actomyosin stress fibers, whereas, under conditions of lower adhesion or extracellular matrix stiffness, cells form smaller more dynamic adhesions.
evidence: Established knowledge about focal adhesion biology

claim: Large adhesions generally promote contractility and cellular quiescence.
source: Large adhesions generally promote contractility and cellular quiescence, while small dynamic adhesions are associated with cell motility and growth.
evidence: Established knowledge about focal adhesion biology

claim: Small dynamic adhesions are associated with cell motility and growth.
source: Large adhesions generally promote contractility and cellular quiescence, while small dynamic adhesions are associated with cell motility and growth.
evidence: Established knowledge about focal adhesion biology

claim: LLPS is driven by highly multivalent, weak interactions between proteins or proteins and RNAs.
source: LLPS is driven by highly multivalent, weak interactions between proteins or proteins and RNAs (Alberti et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Alberti et al., 2019

claim: LLPS domains exhibit rapid exchange of components between droplets and the bulk phase, fusion, and splitting.
source: These domains, also termed 'condensates,' exhibit highly dynamic behaviors, including rapid exchange of components between the droplets and the bulk phase, fusion, and splitting.
evidence: Established knowledge about LLPS properties

claim: LLPS can organize biochemical reactions and regulate gene expression, organelle structure and function, protein synthesis, and mechanotransduction.
source: LLPS can organize biochemical reactions and regulate a wide array of cell functions including gene expression, organelle structure and function, protein synthesis, and mechanotransduction to name a few.
evidence: Established knowledge about LLPS functions

claim: Integrin-mediated adhesions can assemble, grow, split, fuse, and disassemble in live cells.
source: They can assemble, grow, split, fuse, and disassemble in live cells, which often correlate with cell functions such as migration and gene expression (Burridge and Chrzanowska-Wodnicka, 1996; Geiger et al., 2009; Wehrle-Haller, 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Burridge and Chrzanowska-Wodnicka, 1996; Geiger et al., 2009; Wehrle-Haller, 2012

claim: Adhesion components exchange rapidly with the cytoplasm.
source: Adhesion components exchange rapidly with the cytoplasm (Hoffmann et al., 2014; Parsons et al., 2010; Stutchbury et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Hoffmann et al., 2014; Parsons et al., 2010; Stutchbury et al., 2017

claim: p130Cas participates in multivalent interactions and contains extended disordered regions.
source: p130Cas (BCAR1) is an attractive candidate as it participates in multivalent interactions and contains extended disordered regions that often mediate condensate formation (Case et al., 2019; Defilippi et al., 2006; Harte et al., 1996; Polte and Hanks, 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Case et al., 2019; Defilippi et al., 2006; Harte et al., 1996; Polte and Hanks, 1995

claim: Extended disordered regions often mediate condensate formation.
source: p130Cas (BCAR1) is an attractive candidate as it participates in multivalent interactions and contains extended disordered regions that often mediate condensate formation (Case et al., 2019; Defilippi et al., 2006; Harte et al., 1996; Polte and Hanks, 1995).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations

claim: Purified focal adhesion kinase (FAK) forms LLPS in vitro.
source: While these experiments were underway, Case et al., 2022 reported that purified focal adhesion kinase (FAK) forms LLPS in vitro.
evidence: Citation to Case et al., 2022

claim: The addition of paxillin enhances FAK condensates.
source: They further reported that the addition of paxillin enhances FAK condensates; that phosphorylated 130cas, Nck, and N-Wasp also form condensates; and that FAK condensates and p130Cas-Nck-NWasp condensates synergistically recruit paxillin and kindlin-integrin complexes.
evidence: Citation to Case et al., 2022

claim: Phosphorylated p130Cas, Nck, and N-Wasp form condensates.
source: They further reported that the addition of paxillin enhances FAK condensates; that phosphorylated 130cas, Nck, and N-Wasp also form condensates; and that FAK condensates and p130Cas-Nck-NWasp condensates synergistically recruit paxillin and kindlin-integrin complexes.
evidence: Citation to Case et al., 2022

claim: FAK condensates and p130Cas-Nck-NWasp condensates synergistically recruit paxillin and kindlin-integrin complexes.
source: They further reported that the addition of paxillin enhances FAK condensates; that phosphorylated 130cas, Nck, and N-Wasp also form condensates; and that FAK condensates and p130Cas-Nck-NWasp condensates synergistically recruit paxillin and kindlin-integrin complexes.
evidence: Citation to Case et al., 2022

claim: Mutations in FAK and p130Cas that reduce LLPS also reduce adhesion formation in cells.
source: Mutations in FAK and p130Cas that reduce LLPS also reduce adhesion formation in cells.
